sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No, because there is no main image. The page is an online magazine feature (assumed job: pull a general reader into a long story about a community allotment). The byline at about (280, 250) says "Photographs by the residents", but no photograph appears anywhere in the 1280×800 frame. Below the last paragraph (y≈565) the page goes blank for about 225 px. The headline "The allotment at the end of the bus line" sets up a place the reader is never shown. The credit promises pictures the page does not deliver, so the opening reads as text only. For a story whose whole subject is something you can see (beans, squash, pallets, bath tubs, the water tap), that throws away its strongest hook. The empty band suggests a picture that never loaded or sits just below the fold, so check a live browser. The page is fine if a resident's photograph actually appears at the top, or right after the standfirst. If it doesn't, the direction is to put one picture near the headline that adds what the words can't, such as the people at the tap or the beds in their pallets. It should not just show "an allotment" again (the headline already says that). The entry's sources are off the approved list, so this rests on common sense: a credit line for missing photographs is a broken promise to the reader. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- **The headline makes a stranger want to read on.** "The allotment at the end of the bus line" names a specific, slightly odd place. The italic standfirst (y≈285–395) then says what was there before (a car park nobody used), what is there now (forty households), and why to care (the queue for the water tap is "the best place in the district to hear the news"). A first-time reader can say in one sentence what this is and why it's worth reading.
- **The whole page holds one quiet mood.** It uses one sans-serif family, near-black on white, a single hairline under the header, and one muted green for the "Feature" kicker. Nothing decorative competes with the story. The one bit of colour sits on the kicker and fits a gardening story without shouting.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Is the blank band a loading problem?** The empty space below y≈575, together with the photo credit, may mean an image is lazy-loading or failed to load. Check whether a photograph renders on a live page and where it sits.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (main image and headline make one idea together)

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No. The italic standfirst (x 280–1000, y≈285–395) looks only about one pixel larger than the body text below it (y≈420–575), roughly 19 px against 18 px. Its line spacing looks the same, and it is in the same typeface and colour. The italic is the only thing that sets it apart as the introduction. A one-pixel bump doesn't make it read as a bigger level. It just makes the two blocks look slightly mismatched, as if the size was picked by itself. Read top to bottom, the page goes headline, then almost nothing, then body. The standfirst should be the bridge into the story, but it sits nearly at body level. Bringhurst (*Elements*, 3.1.1, "Don't compose without a scale") calls for a small set of clearly distinct sizes. Dair (*Design with Type*, ch. 8) says a contrast meant to be seen must be obvious, not one step. **Fix:** choose one. Either make the standfirst a clear step up on a scale (about 22–24 px, between body and headline) so it reads as the opening level, or set it at exactly the body size and let the italic do all the work. Check the two computed font sizes in a browser. These sizes are by eye. Convention. Weight: minor. The italic already keeps the two blocks apart, so the reader doesn't get lost.

**What's working.** The headline clearly dominates. It is about 44 px heavy bold, more than twice the body size, and nothing else on the screen competes with it, so the eye starts in the right place. The small levels are told apart by colour and weight, not by size. The "Feature" kicker is bold green, the byline is regular grey, and the nav is grey and pushed into the corner, so three near-equal small sizes still read as three different jobs. Keep that: it follows "bolder, not bigger" (Refactoring UI).

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (each level distinct at a glance, with no near-equal sizes)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- Every article element shares one left edge at x≈280: the kicker, headline, byline, standfirst and paragraphs. That single strong edge carries the eye straight down the page. The header sits on a wider container (logo at x=120, nav ending at x=1160) that is centred on the same axis. So the logo's left edge is clearly offset from the article's, with no near-miss, and the two containers read as nested, not competing.
- Spacing steps up with each group. The space under the kicker (about 20 px) is smaller than the space under the headline (about 28 px), which is smaller than the space under the byline (about 33 px). Paragraph gaps (about 18 px) are smaller than all of those but show clearly against about 29 px of leading. So the title block, the standfirst and the body read as separate groups without rules or boxes.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- The bottom band, from about y=580 to 800, is empty. The byline credits "Photographs by the residents", but no picture appears. Check in a live browser whether that space is the end of the capture, a lead image that didn't load, or where the article really stops. If a photo belongs there, its placement against the 280–1000 column can't be judged from this image.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

I've finished the checklist and the reference reading. Here is the report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No. The body paragraphs run from x≈280 to x≈990, which at this size comes to about 85–90 characters per line by eye. For example, "It started with a letter. Halima Osei, who has lived on the estate since 1998, wrote to" is about 87. The italic standfirst (y≈288–395) is about 90 a line. At that width the reader's eye has a long trip back to the start of each line and sometimes lands on the wrong one. This is a long-form feature that depends on easy, unbroken reading, so a too-wide measure slows exactly the reading it exists for. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* 2.1.2, gives 45 to 75 characters and 66 as the ideal. Fix: narrow the text column to about 600 px, or about 66 characters at this size, or raise the body size a little if the column must stay this wide. Check the exact count in a live browser. Convention. Weight: major.
2. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The headline breaks as "…end of the bus / line", leaving "line" alone on the second line (y≈180–220). This splits the noun phrase "bus line" that the title turns on, and a single short word sits under a nearly full line. The headline looks unfinished and its second line reads as a mistake rather than a deliberate stop. Fix: choose the break, for example "The allotment at the end / of the bus line", or use balanced wrapping on the headline so both lines carry a phrase. Bringhurst 2.4 covers keeping units together; a break in a heading isn't confirmed in a source, so this point is common sense. Defect. Weight: minor in function, but it's the first thing on the page, so it's cheap to fix and worth doing.

**What's working.**
- The standfirst is set in a true italic of the same family, at body size and with body leading. That marks it as the deck without a second typeface or a size jump, and four lines of a real text italic stay easy to read.
- Body leading looks about 1.5 (roughly 29 px on 18–19 px type), with paragraphs marked by space alone. The text is calm and even, and the paragraph breaks are clear without indents.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; headings break at phrase boundaries)

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is white with near-black type, gray secondary text and one green accent.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One accent, used once.** The green "Feature" label at about (280, 111) is the only hue on the page. Because nothing else is colored, that small word stands out without needing to be large. It also suits a magazine about growing things. Keep green for this one job. If it spreads to links, the nav or pull quotes, it stops marking anything.
- **Lightness sets the order, not hue.** The headline (about y 130–225) and body text are near-black. The byline (y 251) and nav (top right) are a mid gray. That makes three clear steps of light and dark: headline and body, secondary text, then the white page. The structure would read the same in grayscale. The thin rule under the header at y 61 is pale enough to separate the header without competing with it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the green label, the gray byline and the gray nav meet WCAG 1.4.3 contrast (4.5:1 for small text). All three are small, and the byline gray looks the lightest. Measure their exact colors on the live page. This is a text-contrast question, so it falls under the Text section rather than Color.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. The "Groundwork" wordmark is a logo, and the byline promises photographs.

**Findings**
1. **Does every image show its content, with no broken-image icon or empty placeholder box?** No. The byline at about (280, 250) says "Photographs by the residents," but the first screen has no photograph. The band from about y=580 to 800, between x=200 and 1080, is plain white even at full resolution. There is no faint frame, no broken-image icon and no alt text. A reader is told this is a photo feature about a place: an allotment, beans, squash, a queue at a water tap. What they get is a wall of text with a blank gap below it. Nothing shows them the place, and the residents' photos, which the story credits as theirs, are missing. If a lead image was meant to go here, either it failed to load or the capture caught the page mid-load. If the page really has no picture until further down, the credit promises something the screen doesn't deliver. The checklist has no catalog entry for this line, so this is my own judgment. If the image failed to load, it's a **defect**. If the page is built that way, it's **taste**. **Major** either way, because pictures are the main draw of a feature credited to residents' photographs. Fix: check the live page to see whether an image belongs in that band. If one does, make sure it loads and reserve its space so the gap never shows. If none does, put one strong resident photo of the plot above or right after the standfirst, so the first screen shows the allotment.

**What's working.** The "Groundwork" wordmark at (120, 29) is a plain bold word set in near-black on white. It has generous clear space and no distortion, so it reads at a glance and would hold up small and in one colour. It also stays out of the way of the headline.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty band at y≈580–800 is an image that failed to load or a lazy-load placeholder. Check in a live browser at this viewport, with the cache cleared.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (every image shows its content)

sections.report:
The entries are open, and I'm writing the report now.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a header with a wordmark and four text links (Features, Food, Places, Subscribe). There is nothing else to interact with.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?** The one action the publication most wants, "Subscribe" (x≈1093–1160, y≈31), is styled exactly like the three section links: same grey, size and weight, set off only by a middot. A reader scanning the header sees four equal words, so nothing tells them there is something to sign up for. On a long read, the moment a reader is won over is the moment to catch them, and Subscribe doesn't stand out then.
   - Why: Material Design 3 "Buttons" and NN/g button guidance say one action per view should lead. NN/g, "Flat UI Elements Attract Less Attention" (Moran, 2017), found that links styled like plain text draw less attention.
   - Fix: give Subscribe a button shape (an outline or fill, perhaps in the kicker's green) and move it apart from the section links, so it reads as an action and not a fourth section. It doesn't need to be loud; it needs to be different.
   - Defect. Weight: major for the publication's goals, minor for the reader's.
2. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step, progress, or loading?** The article is labelled "Feature" (green kicker, x≈280, y≈111), but "Features" in the header nav looks the same as Food and Places. The reader can't see which section they are in, or that the kicker and the nav item are the same thing.
   - Why: Laubheimer (NN/g), "Menu-Design Checklist", guideline 5, says this is probably the most common mistake on website menus (Nielsen heuristic 1).
   - Fix: mark the current section in the nav with one cue (bolder weight, an underline, or the kicker green). Also make the kicker and the nav item use the same word, "Feature" or "Features".
   - Defect. Weight: minor.
3. **Do the grouping, names, and navigation show how the product's parts relate?** The header list mixes kinds of thing. "Features" is a story format, "Food" and "Places" are topics, and "Subscribe" is an action. This story, about growing food in a place, could belong under any of the three sections. A reader looking for more pieces like it can't predict where they live.
   - Why: Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, ch. 2 (conceptual model).
   - Fix: use one kind of category for the sections, either all topics or all formats. Set Subscribe apart as an action, which overlaps with finding 1.
   - Taste/common sense, argued from Norman. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The header is conventional and quiet: wordmark top left, nav top right, thin rule below. Readers find their way without thinking, and the chrome stays out of the article's way.
- Nothing covers the content: no cookie banner, sign-up pop-up or sticky bar over the opening of a long read. That keeps the first screen fully readable.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the nav links and the wordmark.
- Whether the header is sticky and would cover focused links or text as the reader scrolls.
- Whether the green "Feature" kicker is a link. If it is, it has no cue showing that.
- Whether the nav links' click area has padding. The text looks about 14 px tall, but the gaps between links probably meet the WCAG 2.5.8 spacing exception.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 28 yes, 3 no (one primary action; shows where the user is; grouping and names show how parts relate), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured)
